interactions.label: During acute inflammation, endothelial cells contract and widen inter-endothelia

params.question: During acute inflammation, endothelial cells contract and widen inter-endothelial gaps, allowing fluid to escape into the interstitium. This fluid is classified as an exudate because it:

answers.text: Is formed by osmotic imbalance and contains less than 2 g/dL protein

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This describes a transudate, which results from hydrostatic or oncotic pressure imbalance without vessel-wall damage. An exudate is driven by active increases in vascular permeability, not pressure gradients.

answers.text: Contains more than 3 g/dL protein due to increased vascular permeability

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Endothelial contraction widens gaps large enough for plasma proteins to escape, producing protein-rich fluid (>3 g/dL) — the hallmark of an inflammatory exudate.

answers.text: Results from hydrostatic pressure imbalance in the venous end of capillaries

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Hydrostatic imbalance, as seen in congestive heart failure, produces a protein-poor transudate (<2 g/dL). The key distinction is that exudates arise from active vascular permeability changes during inflammation.

answers.text: Has a protein content between 1 and 2 g/dL, similar to normal interstitial fluid

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Normal interstitial fluid and transudates have low protein content. An inflammatory exudate, by contrast, exceeds 3 g/dL because inflamed vessels allow large molecules to escape through widened endothelial gaps.

overallFeedback.feedback: The protein content and formation mechanism distinguish exudate from transudate. An exudate (>3 g/dL protein) is produced by increased vascular permeability in inflammation, while a transudate (<2 g/dL) results from hydrostatic or oncotic imbalance without vessel-wall damage.

Correct! The defining feature of an exudate is its high protein content (>3 g/dL), resulting from increased vascular permeability during inflammation — distinguishing it sharply from a low-protein transudate.

interactions.label: Lipoxins, derived from the lipoxygenase pathway, amplify neutrophil recruitment

params.question: Lipoxins, derived from the lipoxygenase pathway, amplify neutrophil recruitment and sustain the inflammatory response.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Lipoxins are indeed products of the lipoxygenase pathway, but unlike leukotrienes (LTB4, LTC4–E4), they are anti-inflammatory. They act as the natural brake on the inflammatory response by inhibiting neutrophil recruitment rather than amplifying it.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Well done. Although lipoxins are derived from the same lipoxygenase pathway as pro-inflammatory leukotrienes, they serve the opposite function — they are the natural brake on inflammation, inhibiting neutrophil recruitment and helping to resolve the response.

interactions.label: A patient on infliximab (anti-TNF-α) therapy for Crohn's disease develops reacti

params.question: A patient on infliximab (anti-TNF-α) therapy for Crohn's disease develops reactivation of latent tuberculosis. Which mechanism best explains this complication?

answers.text: Infliximab directly destroys the epithelioid histiocytes forming the granuloma wall

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Infliximab neutralises circulating TNF-α rather than directly killing cells. Without sustained TNF-α signalling, the granuloma loses structural cohesion, allowing contained mycobacteria to escape — an indirect, not direct, mechanism.

answers.text: TNF-α is required to maintain granuloma integrity; blocking it allows mycobacteria to escape containment

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The Th1–macrophage–TNF-α loop maintains the granuloma. When infliximab neutralises TNF-α, granuloma architecture collapses and dormant bacilli reactivate — hence mandatory TB screening before starting biologics.

answers.text: Anti-TNF-α therapy prevents conversion of M2 macrophages into epithelioid cells

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: It is interferon-gamma from Th1 cells, not TNF-α, that drives the macrophage-to-epithelioid transformation. TNF-α's critical role lies in maintaining granuloma structure once formed, not in initiating epithelioid differentiation.

answers.text: Infliximab blocks interleukin-4, impairing the M1 macrophage response needed to contain TB

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Infliximab targets TNF-α specifically, not IL-4. Moreover, IL-4 drives M2 (repair) polarisation. The M1 (destructive) response depends on interferon-gamma from Th1 cells, not on IL-4 signalling.

overallFeedback.feedback: TNF-α, produced by activated M1 macrophages, is essential for maintaining the granuloma that walls off latent mycobacteria. Infliximab neutralises TNF-α, causing granuloma collapse and reactivation of contained bacilli — the reason mandatory TB screening precedes all anti-TNF-α therapy.
Correct! TNF-α is the key cytokine sustaining granuloma integrity. This is why every patient must be screened for latent TB before starting anti-TNF-α therapy.

interactions.label: Following partial hepatectomy, the remaining liver regenerates to near-normal si

params.question: Following partial hepatectomy, the remaining liver regenerates to near-normal size within weeks. This is possible because hepatocytes are classified as:

answers.text: Labile cells that continuously divide throughout life

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Labile cells (e.g., skin epidermis, gut mucosal epithelium) are in constant replication. Hepatocytes are normally quiescent in G0 but can re-enter the cell cycle when stimulated by growth factors — a defining feature of stable, not labile, cells.

answers.text: Stable cells that re-enter the cell cycle when stimulated, provided the extracellular scaffold is intact

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Hepatocytes are the classic stable (quiescent) cell population. They remain in G0 until stimulated by growth factors, and successful regeneration requires an intact extracellular matrix scaffold to guide new cell placement.

answers.text: Permanent cells that compensate through cellular hypertrophy rather than division

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Permanent cells (neurons, cardiac myocytes) cannot divide and are replaced by scar. The liver grows back through actual cell division (hyperplasia of mature hepatocytes), confirming they are stable, not permanent, cells.

answers.text: Cells that can only regenerate through activation of bone-marrow-derived precursors

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Liver regeneration after partial hepatectomy occurs primarily through re-entry of existing mature hepatocytes into the cell cycle, not through bone-marrow precursors. This ability to shift from G0 to the active cell cycle defines stable cells.

overallFeedback.feedback: Hepatocytes are stable (quiescent) cells that normally reside in G0 but can re-enter the cell cycle when stimulated, provided the extracellular scaffold is intact. This distinguishes them from labile cells (continuously dividing, e.g., gut mucosa) and permanent cells (cannot divide, e.g., neurons, cardiac myocytes).

Correct! Hepatocytes are the classic example of stable cells — quiescent in G0 until growth factors trigger re-entry into the cell cycle, enabling liver regeneration when the extracellular scaffold is preserved.

interactions.label: On gross examination, a pericardial specimen shows a rough, shaggy surface with

params.question: On gross examination, a pericardial specimen shows a rough, shaggy surface with a characteristic 'bread-and-butter' appearance. Which morphological pattern of inflammation does this represent?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Serous inflammation produces thin, watery, protein-poor fluid — as seen in a skin blister or early pleural effusion. It does not deposit the fibrin strands responsible for the shaggy surface texture.

Suppurative (purulent) inflammation generates pus — dead neutrophils and liquefied tissue. When walled off it forms an abscess, as in staphylococcal skin infections. The roughened, shaggy pericardial surface points to fibrin deposition, not pus.

Correct. The bread-and-butter appearance is the hallmark of fibrinous pericarditis, where protein-rich exudate deposits fibrin strands on the pericardial serosa, creating the characteristic roughened, shaggy surface.

Granulomatous inflammation features discrete collections of epithelioid histiocytes and giant cells, as in tuberculosis or sarcoidosis. The bread-and-butter appearance is specific to fibrinous inflammation on serosal surfaces.

overallFeedback.feedback: The bread-and-butter appearance is pathognomonic of fibrinous pericarditis. In this pattern, protein-rich exudate deposits fibrin strands across the serosal surface, distinguishing it from serous (watery), suppurative (pus-filled), and granulomatous (epithelioid cell collections) patterns.
Correct! Fibrinous pericarditis is the classic example of fibrinous inflammation — fibrin strands deposited on the serosal surface create the unmistakable bread-and-butter gross appearance.
